name: Darius the Great
info: Darius I, the third King of Kings of the Achaemenid Empire from 522 to 486 BCE, took the throne by overthrowing Bardiya, suppressed revolts across the empire, reorganised it into satrapies and led it to its greatest extent.

facts.born: c. 550 BCE; the eldest of five sons of Hystaspes, an Achaemenid noble and officer in Cyrus's army, and grandson of Arsames; his mother is variously given as Rhodogune or Irdabama
facts.died: 486 BCE, after thirty days of an unidentified illness, aged about sixty-four; his body was embalmed and entombed in October 486 BCE in the rock-cut tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam
facts.role: Lance-bearer (spearman) to Cambyses II; King of Kings of the Achaemenid Empire from 522 BCE until his death in 486 BCE
facts.known: the killing of Gaumata and the revolts of 522 BCE; the Behistun Inscription; the satrapies and the daric; the Indus Valley and Scythian campaigns; the Darius Canal; the punitive expedition against Eretria and Athens ending at Marathon; the rock-cut tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam

t: Darius became king in 522 BCE by killing the ruler Gaumata, whom he called an impostor; his account of the events is generally regarded as a forgery that concealed the overthrow and murder of Cyrus's rightful successor Bardiya.
He put down revolts in most parts of the empire within a year, divided the empire into twenty satrapies with fixed tributes, and introduced the daric as a universal currency.

His campaigns took the empire to the Indus Valley and into Europe, but the expedition against Athens and Eretria ended in defeat at Marathon in 490 BCE, and he died in 486 BCE while preparing a second.
dyk: At Behistun, Darius had a trilingual inscription in Elamite, Old Persian and Babylonian carved into a cliff-face to record his conquests; it later became a key source for the Old Persian language and for the decipherment of cuneiform.
ev: Darius is born, the eldest son of Hystaspes
With six nobles he kills Gaumata at the fortress of Sikayauvati and takes the throne, then faces revolts in most parts of the empire
He campaigns in Central Asia, Aria and Bactria and winters in Gandhara before conquering the lands around the Indus River in 515 BCE
He crosses the Bosphorus on a bridge of boats and invades European Scythia, where the Scythians avoid battle
He travels to Egypt for the opening of the canal linking the Nile to the Red Sea
The Persian army sent against Athens and Eretria is defeated at the Battle of Marathon
Darius dies after a revolt in Egypt delays his planned expedition; Xerxes succeeds him

sections.early:
Darius was born around 550 BCE, the eldest of five sons of Hystaspes and a grandson of Arsames. His mother's identity is uncertain. According to the modern historian Alireza Shapour Shahbazi (1994), she was thought to have been a woman named Rhodogune; according to Lloyd Llewellyn-Jones (2013), recently uncovered texts from Persepolis indicate that she was Irdabama, an affluent landowner descended from a family of local Elamite rulers, and Richard Stoneman likewise names Irdabama. Hystaspes was an officer in Cyrus's army and a noble of his court. The Behistun Inscription of Darius states that he was satrap of Bactria in 522 BCE and a second cousin of Cyrus in the paternal line, though this may have been a fabrication to legitimate Darius's accession.

According to Herodotus (III.139), Darius, “of no consequence at the time”, served as a spearman (doryphoros) in the Egyptian campaign of Cambyses II (528–525 BCE); this is often interpreted to mean that he was the king's personal spear-carrier, an important role. Darius's own account likewise says that he served Cambyses as lance-bearer. A story told of Cyrus relates that, before crossing the river Araxes, he installed his son Cambyses as king and then dreamed that Darius had wings on his shoulders and stood upon the confines of Europe and Asia. Cyrus took this as a danger to the empire, wondered whether Darius was forming treasonable designs, and ordered Hystaspes back to Persis to watch his son strictly.
sections.rise:
The sources give different accounts of how Darius came to the throne. The oldest records report that Cambyses II lost his mind, had his brother Bardiya murdered and died of an infected leg wound, after which Darius and six nobles went to Sikayauvati to kill a usurper, Gaumata, who had taken the throne by pretending to be Bardiya. In Darius's own account, written at Behistun, the murder of Bardiya was not known among the Iranians; a revolt against Cambyses broke out in his absence on 11 March 522 BCE, and on 1 July the people chose to be under Gaumata as “Bardiya”. No member of the Achaemenid family would rise against him for fear for their lives. Darius, praying for aid, killed Gaumata in September 522 BCE with Otanes, Intaphrenes, Gobryas, Hydarnes, Megabyzus and Aspathines.

Herodotus's account is dubious. The seven nobles debated the form of government, with Otanes urging a democratic republic, Megabyzus an oligarchy and Darius a monarchy, and then settled the matter by whose horse neighed first at sunrise. In Herodotus's telling, Darius's groom Oebares arranged for Darius's horse to neigh. Greek historians also say that Gaumata was a Magian placed on the throne by his brother Patizeithes after Bardiya's murder. The details of Darius's rise are generally acknowledged as forgery, used to conceal his overthrow and murder of Cyrus's rightful successor, Bardiya. To legitimise his rule he had a common origin with Cyrus fabricated by naming Achaemenes as founder of their dynasty; he was not from the house of Cyrus and his forebears, the rulers of Anshan.
sections.deeds:
Early in his reign Darius reorganised the empire and the taxation he had inherited from Cyrus and Cambyses. He created twenty provinces called satrapies, each under a satrap and each with a fixed tribute, paid in silver measured by the Babylonian talent and in gold measured by the Euboic talent; the total from the satraps came to less than 15,000 silver talents. Persis was the only province that was not conquered land. Each satrap had a secretary, a treasurer and a garrison commander, and royal inspectors, the “eyes and ears” of Darius, checked on them. Aramaic was kept as the common language. Before 500 BCE he introduced the daric, a gold and silver coin that replaced barter and Lydian or Ionian coins and that was also recognised beyond the empire's borders. He improved the network of roads and way stations, built canals and a navy, and in 497 BCE travelled to Egypt to open the canal that joined the Nile to the Red Sea.

His campaigns reached the empire's territorial apex. In 516 BCE he marched through Central Asia, Aria and Bactria to Gandhara, wintered there, and in 515 BCE conquered the lands around the Indus River, appointing the Greek Scylax of Caryanda to explore the Indian Ocean from the mouth of the Indus to Suez. In 513 BCE he invaded European Scythia, and he then took Thrace and many cities of the northern Aegean. He built or expanded works at Susa, Persepolis, Babylon and in Egypt, where he built and restored temples, among them those to Ptah and Nekhbet. These works employed workers and artisans of many nationalities, several of them deportees.
sections.opponents:
By late 522 BCE there were revolts in most parts of the empire. They broke out in Elam and Babylonia, then Bactria, Persis, Media, Parthia, Assyria and Egypt. Darius had a loyal army led by close confidants and nobles, and with their support suppressed all of them within a year. In his own words he killed nine “lying kings”, whom he depicted in the Behistun Inscription. The Elamite leader Aschina was captured and executed at Susa. The Babylonian revolt, led by Nebuchadnezzar III, held out against a large army for a year and a half, and the Scythian king Skunkha was captured and added to the rebels shown at Behistun. His reign also had killings among his own supporters. When the noble Intaphernes mutilated two officers who barred him from the palace, Darius feared a revolt of the seven, had Intaphernes arrested with his son, relatives and friends able to bear arms, and, though no proof of a plan was found, killed his entire family except his wife's brother and her son. In Egypt he executed Aryandes on a charge of treason.

Abroad, the Scythians evaded his army in 513 BCE by feints, retreats and a scorched-earth strategy, and Darius ordered a halt after a month of losses to fatigue, privation and sickness. The Ionian Revolt, in which Eretria and Athens sent ships and troops and burned Sardis, brought the Persian reoccupation of the Ionian and Greek islands, and a force Darius sent across the Hellespont was turned back by a storm and the Thracians. His army, 20,000 men under Datis and Artaphernes, took Eretria but was defeated at Marathon in 490 BCE.
sections.last:
After the defeat at Marathon, Darius began planning another expedition against the Greek city-states, this time to command the imperial armies himself instead of leaving them to Datis. He spent three years preparing men and ships when a revolt broke out in Egypt. The revolt worsened his failing health and prevented him from leading another army.

Darius died after thirty days of suffering from an unidentified illness, partly due to his part in crushing the revolt, at about sixty-four years old. In October 486 BCE his body was embalmed and entombed in the rock-cut tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam, which he had been preparing. Its inscription introduces him as “Great King, King of Kings, King of countries containing all kinds of men, King in this great earth far and wide, son of Hystaspes, an Achaemenian, a Persian, son of a Persian, an Aryan, having Aryan lineage.” A relief beneath the tomb showing equestrian combat was carved later, under the Sasanian King of Kings Bahram II.

Darius had several wives, among them Atossa and Artystone, daughters of Cyrus, and Parmys, a daughter of Bardiya. His eldest son, Artobazanes, was born to a daughter of Gobryas before Darius rose to power. Xerxes, his eldest son by Atossa, became heir through her influence, since she had great authority in the kingdom and Darius loved her most of all his wives. Xerxes had contested the succession with Artobazanes and became king as Xerxes I, so that the empire was again ruled by a member of the house of Cyrus. Xerxes completed the construction projects still under way.
sections.legacy:
Darius ruled the empire at its territorial peak, when it included much of West Asia, parts of the Balkans and the Caucasus, most of the Black Sea's coastal regions, Central Asia, the Indus Valley and parts of North Africa and Northeast Africa, including Egypt. His changes in provincial administration, coinage, weights and measures, roads and language made the empire centralised and unified. The daric was a major boost to international trade, and the new tax system led to the registration of measured and taxed land and to state banking and banking firms, one of the most famous being Murashu Sons of Nippur.

He supported the faiths of the lands he ruled so long as their adherents were “submissive and peaceable”, sometimes with grants from his treasury; he funded the restoration of the Israelite temple originally decreed by Cyrus, wrote to Gadatas in support of Greek cults, supported Elamite priests and built a temple to the Egyptian god Amun. His own faith was in Ahura Mazda, whom he believed had appointed him; he held that each rebellion was the work of druj, the enemy of Asha, and wrote “Ahura Mazda is mine, I am Ahura Mazda's”. Scholars have no consensus on whether he and his predecessors were influenced by Zoroastrianism.

His inscriptions are a main source for his reign: the Behistun Inscription later became a key source for the Old Persian language and for the decipherment of cuneiform, and Greek historiography, above all Herodotus, who gave him half of Book 3 and Books 4 to 6, records his campaigns against the Scythians and Greeks.

summary: Darius I (c. 550–486 BCE) became King of the Achaemenid Empire in 522 BCE by killing Gaumata, an account historians generally regard as a cover for the overthrow of Bardiya. He suppressed revolts, organised the empire into satrapies, issued the daric and reached its greatest extent, but was defeated at Marathon.
references: Pierre Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander: A History of the Persian Empire (Eisenbrauns, 2002)
A. Kuhrt, The Persian Empire: A Corpus of Sources from the Achaemenid Period (Routledge, 2013)
Lloyd Llewellyn-Jones, King and Court in Ancient Persia 559 to 331 BCE (Edinburgh University Press, 2013)
notes: Birth: the lede says c. 550 BCE and the death account says about sixty-four, which agree. Start set circa true.
Death year 486 BCE; entombment in October 486 BCE. The article gives no day or place of death.
Mother: Rhodogune (Shahbazi 1994) or Irdabama (Llewellyn-Jones 2013, Stoneman); both given, in facts.born simply 'variously given'.

Hystaspes as second cousin of Cyrus is from Behistun and 'may have been a fabrication'; stated as such. The article spells Intaphrenes in the Behistun list and Intaphernes later, and Artobazanes and Artobarzanes; the first spelling of each is used where the article uses it.

Egypt: the article suggests the Egyptian rebellion listed at Behistun may be a scribal error, with the rebel possibly Petubastis III; left out. The article does not date Darius's Egyptian revolt of the last years beyond 'three years of preparation' after Marathon.

Left out: the horse-and-groom statue inscription detail beyond Oebares; the Zopyrus and mule story of the Babylon siege (told 'according to the story'); Darius the Mede and the film portrayal (not relevant); the Aryan script created by scholars.
Intaphernes: the Herodotean story of his wife's choice is left out; the killing of the family is stated as the article gives it.
The 'revolts within a year' and 'nine lying kings' are from the article's text on Darius's own account.

Event 497 BCE: the article gives 497 BCE for the visit and opening of the canal; deeds mentions the same. The article does not give the year of the Ionian Revolt or Sardis burning, so no event for it.
Slight overlap: the final sentence of opponents repeats the forgery point; the editor may trim it.
